messages.content: I want to generate synchronized audio from silent video, but the system should distinguish sound events that are visually determined from sound alternatives that remain acoustically ambiguous.

The goal has two parts: produce audio that aligns with the silent video's visible events, and preserve uncertainty where the visuals do not determine a unique sound. A visible event can constrain when an associated sound begins without necessarily settling every aspect of what that sound should be.
So synchronization and ambiguity are both part of the goal, rather than competing descriptions of it?

Yes. Synchronization concerns the relationship between generated audio and visible events. Acoustically ambiguous alternatives concern cases where more than one sound remains plausible. Keeping alternatives open does not mean treating the timing of a visible event as unconstrained.
What is the specific timing requirement?

The target is to reduce visible-event audio onset error by 20% versus an equally sized deterministic video-to-audio baseline. That comparison is about onset error for visible events, not a claim that every property of the generated audio improves by 20%.
Is that a relative reduction or a decrease of 20 percentage points?

It is a 20% reduction versus the baseline. Expressed abstractly, if the baseline's visible-event audio onset error is E, the target is an error no greater than 0.8E. The goal does not give a measured value for E or specify an onset-error unit.
Why does the comparison specify an equally sized baseline?

That qualification is part of the stated comparison: the baseline is an equally sized deterministic video-to-audio system. The goal does not define what measure of size is intended, so it would be premature to substitute a particular one.
And what does deterministic mean in that comparison?

In general, deterministic means that the same input yields the same output under the same conditions. Here it identifies the video-to-audio baseline for the onset-error comparison; it does not, by itself, specify its architecture or how its size is measured.
I also want the alternative sounds taken seriously. What is the coverage target?

The target is to cover 90% of reference-supported sound alternatives across samples. The word “reference-supported” matters: the target concerns alternatives supported by the references, not arbitrary sounds one might imagine for a silent video.
Does 90% mean that every individual sample must contain nearly all of its possible sounds?

The requirement says “across samples.” It states an aggregate coverage target for reference-supported sound alternatives; it does not say that every alternative must appear in a single generated soundtrack or impose a separate 90% threshold on each individual sample.
Could the system meet that coverage goal simply by generating lots of different events?

Coverage is not the only constraint. Visually contradicted events must remain below 5%. The aim is to account for reference-supported alternatives while avoiding events that conflict with the visual evidence, not to increase variety without regard to the video.
What distinction should I keep in mind between an ambiguous sound and a visually contradicted event?

An ambiguous alternative is one the visual evidence does not uniquely settle and that has reference support. A visually contradicted event conflicts with what the video shows. Those are different conditions: uncertainty about sound does not make every proposed event acceptable.
If an event is clearly visible, does that mean its sound is fully determined?

Not necessarily. The video may establish that an event occurs, and may constrain its timing, while leaving aspects of the associated audio uncertain. The goal is to distinguish what the visuals determine from what remains acoustically ambiguous rather than assuming that visible certainty always implies a unique sound.
Is the below-5% condition a softer aspiration than the 90% coverage target?

Both are stated requirements. The coverage target is 90% of reference-supported sound alternatives across samples, and visually contradicted events are to be below 5%. The wording gives a strict “below” condition for the latter; it does not provide a more detailed definition of that percentage's denominator.
I don't want the alternatives to make the audio feel detached from the visible sequence.

That concern fits the goal. Alternatives should represent acoustic uncertainty without discarding synchronization with visually determined events. In particular, the explicit timing target remains the 20% reduction in visible-event audio onset error relative to the equally sized deterministic video-to-audio baseline.
Does covering alternatives mean declaring one of them to be the true sound of the silent video?

No. A silent video can leave the audio underdetermined. The requirement is to cover reference-supported sound alternatives across samples while distinguishing them from visually determined events; it does not say that one acoustically ambiguous alternative must be presented as uniquely true.
And these are targets, not results already established?
Correct. The node sets the goal and its requirements. It does not report an achieved onset-error reduction, measured alternative coverage, or an observed rate of visually contradicted events.
Then the two numbers address different risks: poor timing and too narrow a treatment of plausible sounds?

Yes, with one more constraint alongside coverage. The 20% comparison addresses visible-event audio onset error. The 90% target addresses coverage of reference-supported sound alternatives across samples. Keeping visually contradicted events below 5% limits alternatives that conflict with the video.
So an alternative being acoustically plausible is not enough on its own?

Right. For the stated coverage target, the alternative must be reference-supported. It also must not be treated as a license to generate visually contradicted events. Acoustic ambiguity calls for distinguishing supported possibilities from what the visual evidence rules out.
How would you approach the goal of aligning audio to visible events while still allowing sound alternatives when the video is ambiguous?

One proposal is to train event-anchored audio diffusion with frame-level onset supervision and uncertainty-conditioned sampling, gated against visually contradicted events. The event anchoring and onset supervision address alignment with what is visible; uncertainty-conditioned sampling leaves room for acoustically ambiguous alternatives; the gate limits alternatives that conflict with the video.
What does “event-anchored” mean here?

It means the proposed audio generation is organized around events identified in the video, rather than treating the video only as an undifferentiated prompt. The proposal does not specify how those events are represented or identified.
Is an anchor supposed to determine the exact sound of an event?

No. An event anchor can constrain the relationship between an audible event and a visible one without uniquely determining how the event sounds. That distinction matters because the proposal is meant to retain acoustically ambiguous alternatives.
Then what role does frame-level onset supervision play?

It supplies training guidance about when an audio event begins at the level of video frames. The intended emphasis is on onset alignment with visible events. The proposal does not specify a labeling procedure, a time tolerance, or how onset supervision is combined with other training signals.
Why focus on onsets rather than just whether the right kind of sound is present?

Presence alone would not express whether a sound begins in step with a visible event. Frame-level onset supervision addresses that temporal distinction. It is part of the proposed way to pursue synchronized audio, not evidence that a particular degree of timing improvement has already been achieved.
Does frame-level supervision imply that every audible event has a visually obvious start?

No. It describes the proposed granularity of onset guidance, not a claim that every sound has an unambiguous visible onset. The approach still needs to distinguish visually determined events from aspects of the audio that the video leaves uncertain.
Where does audio diffusion fit into the proposal?

Audio diffusion is the proposed generative component. In this proposal, it is event-anchored and trained with frame-level onset supervision, while its sampling is conditioned on uncertainty and constrained against visually contradicted events. Those phrases describe the approach, but they do not specify a diffusion architecture or sampling algorithm.
What does uncertainty-conditioned sampling add that event anchoring does not?

Event anchoring connects generated audio to visible events. Uncertainty-conditioned sampling addresses the separate question of how to handle sound aspects the video does not settle uniquely. It is meant to permit supported alternatives where there is acoustic ambiguity without treating every aspect of every event as equally uncertain.
Does that mean the system always generates multiple soundtracks?

Not necessarily. The proposal says sampling is uncertainty-conditioned; it does not prescribe a fixed number of outputs or say that multiple alternatives must be presented for every video. Its point is that ambiguity can influence sampling rather than being ignored.
How would the system know how uncertain a sound is?

That is not specified in this proposal. “Uncertainty-conditioned” identifies the intended role of uncertainty in sampling, but it does not define a particular uncertainty estimate, source, representation, or calibration method.
And what exactly is being gated?

The proposed sampling is gated against visually contradicted events. Conceptually, the gate constrains which generated events are acceptable in light of the video. The proposal does not state a particular gate mechanism, decision threshold, or stage at which it operates.
Is the gate meant to eliminate all acoustic variation?

No. Its target is visual contradiction, not variation itself. An alternative can remain acoustically ambiguous without being contradicted by the visuals. The proposal pairs uncertainty-conditioned sampling with the gate precisely so that allowing alternatives need not mean allowing visually inconsistent events.
Could the onset guidance and the gate end up doing the same job?

They address different questions. Frame-level onset supervision concerns when audio begins relative to visible events. Gating against visually contradicted events concerns whether a candidate event conflicts with what is shown. A sound could be timed to a visible moment yet still depict an event the video contradicts, so timing guidance alone does not express the gate's role.
Could a plausible sound still be rejected by the gate?

In principle, yes: acoustic plausibility by itself is not the same as consistency with the video. The proposed gate is specifically against visually contradicted events. That does not imply rejecting an alternative merely because the video leaves its precise sound unresolved.
Should I read “train event-anchored audio diffusion” as a report that this model has already been trained?

No. It is a proposed approach: train event-anchored audio diffusion, use frame-level onset supervision, and make sampling uncertainty-conditioned with a gate against visually contradicted events. It does not report a completed training run or measured performance.
Is there a specified way to combine the frame-level onset guidance and uncertainty conditioning?

Not in this proposal. It names both as components of the approach, but leaves their precise interaction open. The distinction to preserve is that onset guidance addresses temporal anchoring, while uncertainty conditioning addresses alternatives the visual evidence does not uniquely resolve.
So the proposal does not require choosing between tight synchronization and acknowledging ambiguity?

Correct. It proposes training around visible-event timing while conditioning sampling on uncertainty. The gate adds a boundary: ambiguity may support different sounds, but not events that are visually contradicted. Whether this combination meets the goal's requirements remains to be established.
How can sampling preserve frame-accurate visible-event onsets while exploring plausible sounds without generating visually contradicted events?

The key distinction is between what the video constrains and what it leaves open. Sampling should not move an onset that is tied to a visible event merely to explore a different sound. At the same time, it should not treat the visible event as specifying every acoustic detail. Any explored alternative also has to remain consistent with what the video shows. That describes the problem to solve, not a demonstrated method for solving it.
Is this mainly a question about when variation is allowed?

Yes, though it is also about what may vary. The question asks how to preserve frame-accurate onset timing for visible events while allowing plausible acoustic variation, and how to keep that variation from turning into a visually contradicted event. Those constraints have to hold together during sampling.
Could sampling keep the visible-event onset fixed but explore different sounds around it?

That is the conceptual distinction the question points toward: onset timing may be constrained by the visible event even when the resulting sound is not uniquely determined. But saying that does not yet specify how a sampler would maintain frame accuracy, or which alternatives it would admit.
What would count as losing the onset constraint?

Conceptually, an output would lose it if the audio associated with a visible event began at a different frame from the onset it was meant to follow. The question is about preventing that sort of timing drift while sampling alternatives; it does not supply a measurement rule or an acceptable timing tolerance.
Does frame-accurate mean all sounds in the video must begin at visually identifiable frames?
No. The question specifically concerns visible-event onsets. It does not claim that every possible sound has a visible cause or that every sound's start can be read unambiguously from the frames.
Could a sound be plausible in isolation but still be a bad sample for a particular video?

Yes. Plausibility as audio is not enough: a proposed event can conflict with what is visible. The question asks how to explore plausible sounds without generating those visually contradicted events, rather than treating any believable sound as suitable.
Is a visually contradicted event the same thing as an acoustically ambiguous alternative?

No. An acoustically ambiguous alternative is a possibility the visual evidence does not uniquely settle. A visually contradicted event is incompatible with that evidence. The difficult part is allowing the former during sampling without admitting the latter.
Would preserving the onset alone prevent visual contradictions?

Not necessarily. A generated event could begin at the right visible moment yet still conflict with what the video depicts. Timing consistency and event consistency are separate checks in the question.
And could rejecting contradictions alone protect the timing?

Not necessarily. An event might be consistent with the video in kind but start too early or too late relative to its visible onset. Avoiding visual contradiction does not by itself establish frame-accurate alignment.
So where does the earlier event-anchored audio diffusion proposal enter this question?

It provides the proposed setting: event-anchored audio diffusion with frame-level onset supervision and uncertainty-conditioned sampling gated against visually contradicted events. The open question here is how sampling in that setting can honor the visible-event onset constraint while exploring plausible sounds and excluding visual contradictions. The proposal's components name the intended roles, but do not by themselves answer how reliably those roles can be enforced together.
Does frame-level onset supervision guarantee that a sampled output will be frame-accurate?

No guarantee is stated. Supervision describes training guidance; the question asks what happens during sampling, when acoustic alternatives are explored. It remains open whether that guidance alone would keep each sampled onset aligned.
Could uncertainty-conditioned sampling accidentally change something the video actually determines?

That is one of the tensions behind the question. If uncertainty is applied too broadly, variation could affect an onset or an event that should be constrained by the visuals. The question does not specify how to delineate uncertain acoustic aspects from visually determined ones.
Is the gate supposed to decide whether a sound is the uniquely correct one?

No. Gating against visually contradicted events is different from declaring one sound uniquely correct. Where several sounds remain plausible, the gate's stated concern is whether an event conflicts with the video, not whether it is the only possible audio interpretation.
What if the video simply cannot distinguish between two candidate sounds?

Then visual evidence alone would not settle which sound to choose. The question is how sampling can explore plausible alternatives in such a case while preserving any onset the visible event does determine and avoiding events the visuals contradict. It does not specify a rule for ranking the candidates.
Am I asking for a particular sampling algorithm here?

Not yet. The question identifies the behavior a sampling approach would need to reconcile: frame-accurate visible-event onsets, exploration of plausible sounds, and exclusion of visually contradicted events. It does not commit to a particular algorithm, constraint mechanism, or sequence of decisions.
Then the unresolved point is whether those three demands can be kept separate in the output?

More precisely, it is how they can be maintained together. The onset of a visible event should remain aligned, ambiguity should still permit plausible sound alternatives, and neither timing alignment nor acoustic plausibility should be mistaken for proof that a generated event is visually consistent. The question remains open rather than asserting that sampling already achieves all three.
What outcome would support the idea that event-anchored, uncertainty-sampled, visually gated diffusion can handle timing and ambiguity together?

The hypothesis is that this approach yields at least 20% lower onset mean absolute error (MAE) than deterministic audio, at least 90% alternative recall, and fewer than 5% visual contradictions. Those are predicted outcomes, not reported results.
Does the timing claim refer to an absolute 20-point difference?

No. “At least 20% lower onset MAE than deterministic audio” is a relative comparison. If the deterministic comparator has onset MAE E, the hypothesized outcome is at most 0.8E. The hypothesis does not provide a measured value for E or a unit for the error.
Why specify onset MAE rather than just saying the audio is synchronized?

Onset MAE names a particular timing measure: mean absolute error in when sounds begin. “Synchronized” is broader and could describe other aspects of timing. The hypothesis makes a specific prediction about onset error, in the context of aligning audio with visible events.
Is the 20% improvement meant to say that every sampled sound begins more accurately?
No. A lower MAE is an aggregate error claim; it does not say that every individual onset improves. The hypothesis also does not specify how onset errors would be distributed across samples.
What is the separate claim about alternatives?

It predicts alternative recall of at least 90%. That is meant to capture whether sampling retains the relevant sound alternatives, rather than producing well-timed audio only by narrowing everything to one possibility. It is a recall claim, not a statement that every generated sound is an appropriate alternative.
Could high alternative recall just mean admitting many sounds that the video rules out?

That is why the hypothesis also sets visual contradictions below 5%. It predicts both broad alternative recall and a low rate of visually contradicted events. Neither condition should be read as replacing the other.
If alternative recall reaches 90%, does that imply visual contradictions are below 5%?

No. Recall and visual contradictions measure different things. Recovering alternatives does not, by itself, establish that generated events are visually consistent. The hypothesis asserts both thresholds separately.
And does fewer than 5% visual contradictions mean no contradictory event can ever appear?
No. “Fewer than 5%” allows for a nonzero rate; it does not claim perfect exclusion. The hypothesis does not specify the denominator or a more detailed counting rule for that percentage.
Are the inequalities important here?

Yes. The prediction is ≥20% lower onset MAE than deterministic audio, ≥90% alternative recall, and <5% visual contradictions. Exactly 90% recall meets its stated threshold, whereas exactly 5% visual contradictions does not meet the strict below-5% condition.
What does “uncertainty-sampled” contribute to the hypothesis?

It identifies the proposed way to explore plausible sounds where the video leaves acoustic uncertainty. The hypothesis is that this exploration can coexist with event-anchored timing and visual gating. It does not say how uncertainty is represented or how many alternatives are sampled.
What is the role of the event anchor in that prediction?

The event anchor connects generated audio to visible events, particularly for the onset-alignment part of the prediction. It does not imply that the video determines a unique sound for each event. The predicted reduction in onset MAE is a claim to be assessed, not something the word “anchored” guarantees.
Likewise, does calling the diffusion visually gated establish the contradiction rate?

No. “Visually gated” describes the proposed constraint against events that conflict with the video. The <5% visual-contradiction rate is the hypothesized outcome; naming a gate does not demonstrate that it achieves that rate.
Does the hypothesis specify exactly which deterministic audio system is used for the MAE comparison?

It specifies the comparator as deterministic audio, but does not describe that system's architecture, training, or measured MAE. The numerical statement is the predicted relative reduction in onset MAE against that comparator.
Could the approach satisfy the timing prediction while failing the overall hypothesis?

Yes. The hypothesis combines three predictions. A result with at least 20% lower onset MAE would address the timing prediction, but the stated hypothesis would still require at least 90% alternative recall and fewer than 5% visual contradictions.
And could it meet both percentage thresholds for alternatives and contradictions but miss the timing prediction?

Yes. High alternative recall and a low contradiction rate would not establish the hypothesized onset-MAE improvement. The three measures jointly express the intended balance between timing, acoustic alternatives, and visual consistency.
So this is a testable answer to the sampling question, not an assertion that the tension has already been resolved?

Exactly. It proposes that event-anchored, uncertainty-sampled, visually gated diffusion can achieve those three outcomes together. The hypothesis does not report measurements or establish that sampling already preserves onset accuracy while exploring alternatives.
What plan would let us examine whether sampling can keep visible-event onsets aligned while exploring plausible sounds without visual contradictions?

The plan is to annotate multi-reference clips, train uncertainty-conditioned, event-anchored audio diffusion with visual gating, and compare onset mean absolute error (MAE), alternative recall, and visual-contradiction rate against a matched baseline. Those three comparisons address timing, coverage of alternatives, and consistency with the video, respectively.
Why start with multi-reference clips?

Multiple references make it possible to consider more than one supported sound for a clip when the video does not uniquely determine the audio. Annotating those clips provides a basis for examining alternatives as well as visible-event onsets. The plan does not specify the number of references per clip or the annotation procedure.
Does “multi-reference” mean all the references must sound alike?
No. The point of having multiple references is that they can represent supported possibilities for a clip. The plan does not say how similar or different those references must be.
What would the annotations need to contribute to the comparison?

Conceptually, the comparison needs a way to assess onset timing, which alternatives are supported, and whether a generated event contradicts the video. The plan says to annotate multi-reference clips, but it does not prescribe annotation fields, labeling rules, or how disagreements would be handled.
Are you assuming that every reference settles the precise onset of every sound?

No. That would add an assumption the plan does not make. The plan calls for annotations and an onset-MAE comparison, without specifying which onsets are annotatable or how uncertainty in an onset annotation would be treated.
After annotation, what is trained?

Uncertainty-conditioned, event-anchored audio diffusion with visual gating. In the plan, event anchoring addresses the connection to visible events, uncertainty conditioning allows sampling to reflect acoustic ambiguity, and visual gating constrains events that conflict with what is shown. The precise training procedure and model design are not specified.
Is visual gating another name for onset alignment?

No. Onset alignment concerns when audio begins relative to a visible event. Visual gating concerns whether a generated event is consistent with the video's content. The plan includes both because a well-timed sound could still represent a visually contradicted event.
Could visual gating remove all the alternatives and still make the system look successful?

That is why alternative recall is included in the comparison. A low contradiction rate alone would not show that the system preserves supported alternatives. The plan evaluates both, alongside onset MAE, rather than relying on one measure to stand in for all three.
What exactly will onset MAE tell us?

It will compare the magnitude of onset-timing errors on average. Within this plan, it is the timing measure for the trained approach and the matched baseline. Onset MAE by itself would not tell us whether plausible alternatives are represented or whether generated events contradict the video.
And what will alternative recall tell us that onset MAE cannot?

Alternative recall concerns how much of the reference-supported range of sounds is covered. A system could align the sound it produces very closely with visible events yet represent too few supported alternatives. The plan keeps that question separate from onset timing.
How should I read the contradiction rate in this set of comparisons?

It concerns generated events that conflict with what the video shows. It helps distinguish exploration of plausible acoustic alternatives from generation of visually inconsistent events. The plan names the rate as a comparison measure but does not define its counting rule or denominator.
Does the plan say the model will be compared with an unrelated audio generator?
No. It says the comparison is against a matched baseline. It does not specify the matching criteria or the baseline's implementation, so those details should not be inferred from the plan.
Why compare all three measures against the baseline rather than report just one overall score?

The measures answer distinct parts of the question. Onset MAE addresses timing; alternative recall addresses whether plausible, reference-supported options are retained; contradiction rate addresses conflicts with the visuals. A single timing score, for example, could not show how the system handles ambiguity.
Is the annotation stage itself an experiment showing that uncertainty conditioning works?

No. Annotation prepares the multi-reference clips for training and comparison. Whether uncertainty-conditioned sampling helps with alternatives while maintaining timing and visual consistency is what the planned evaluation is meant to examine; no outcome is reported here.
Does the order matter: annotate, train, then compare?

That is the order stated in the plan. The annotated multi-reference clips support the subsequent training and assessment, and the three measures are then compared against the matched baseline. The plan does not give a schedule or specify how the clips are divided between those activities.
Could the comparison tell us that one part improves while another gets worse?

Yes. Keeping the measures separate makes such a trade-off visible in principle. The plan does not predict what any of the measured values will be; it specifies what to compare so that timing, alternatives, and contradictions can each be examined.
Do we have to settle on a particular way of estimating uncertainty before stating this plan?

Not to state the plan as written. It calls for training uncertainty-conditioned diffusion, but leaves the uncertainty representation and estimation method unspecified. Those would be implementation details, not facts supplied by this plan.
And does “event-anchored” tell us how the model detects an event in the frames?

No. It says that the proposed diffusion model is anchored to events, but does not specify how events are identified, encoded, or associated with onsets. The plan's comparison of onset MAE would assess timing behavior without itself defining that internal mechanism.
So this is a way to investigate the sampling question, rather than a claim that the trained system already passes it?

Exactly. The plan is to annotate multi-reference clips, train the uncertainty-conditioned, event-anchored diffusion model with visual gating, and compare onset MAE, alternative recall, and contradiction rate against a matched baseline. It states the work and the measures, not completed training or results.
For the annotation part, what exactly is the activity?

Annotate 1,200 SilentSound-MR clips with visible-event onset frames, reference-supported sound alternatives, and visually contradicted event labels. That specifies the clip count and the three kinds of annotation; it does not report that the annotations have been completed.
The number is 1,200 clips, not 1,200 onset frames?

Correct. The activity covers 1,200 SilentSound-MR clips. Visible-event onset frames are one kind of information to annotate within that set of clips; the statement does not specify how many onsets there are.
What is meant by a visible-event onset frame?

It is a frame marking when a visible event begins. In this activity, those frames provide the visual timing annotations. The activity does not specify a rule for choosing a frame when an event's beginning is difficult to distinguish.
Are those frames supposed to tell us exactly what sound to use?

No. An onset frame identifies timing for a visible event; it does not necessarily determine that event's precise sound. The reference-supported sound alternatives are annotated separately to represent possibilities supported by the references.
Why say “reference-supported” rather than simply “plausible”?

Because the annotation activity is specifically about alternatives supported by the references. A sound might seem plausible in general without being one of the reference-supported alternatives being labeled. The activity does not replace reference support with an annotator's unrestricted imagination.
Does annotating alternatives mean picking just one preferred sound for each clip?

No. The wording calls for sound alternatives, so the activity is not framed as choosing a single preferred sound in every case. It does not prescribe how many supported alternatives any particular clip has or how they are represented in the annotations.
And what are the visually contradicted event labels for?

They identify events that conflict with what the clip visibly shows. That is a different annotation from recording a sound alternative supported by the references: an acoustically conceivable event should not be treated as an acceptable alternative if it is visually contradicted.
If a sound is not visibly determined, should it automatically receive a contradiction label?

No. Not being uniquely determined by the video is different from being contradicted by it. The activity distinguishes reference-supported sound alternatives from visually contradicted events rather than treating all visual uncertainty as contradiction.
What if the video does not clearly establish whether a particular sound occurred?

That uncertainty alone does not establish a visual contradiction. The stated labels concern visually contradicted events, while the alternatives concern sounds supported by the references. The activity does not give a detailed rule for borderline cases, so it would be premature to assign one here.
Could an onset-frame annotation and a sound-alternative annotation refer to the same visible event?

Conceptually, yes: the visible event may constrain when associated audio begins while the references support more than one way it could sound. The activity names both forms of annotation but does not specify a linking format between them.
Why keep the contradiction labels separate from the alternatives?

They express different relationships to the evidence. A reference-supported alternative records a supported acoustic possibility; a visually contradicted event label records a conflict with the video. Keeping those distinctions explicit makes it possible to discuss variation without treating visually inconsistent events as ordinary alternatives.
Does the activity specify who will annotate the clips?
No. It specifies 1,200 SilentSound-MR clips and the three annotation categories, but not the annotators, their instructions, or an adjudication process.
Does it specify how the references are provided or how many each clip has?

No. The activity requires reference-supported sound alternatives, but it does not state the number of references per clip or the format in which they are supplied. Those details should not be inferred from the dataset name.
Are the contradiction labels judgments about whether generated audio sounds realistic?
Not as stated. They are labels for visually contradicted events—whether an event conflicts with the visual evidence. A judgment about general acoustic realism would be a different criterion.
Could an audio event start at the annotated onset frame yet still fall under a visually contradicted event label?

In principle, yes. Matching a visible-event onset frame addresses timing, while visual contradiction concerns what event the audio depicts. Correct timing alone does not establish that the depicted event is consistent with the clip.
Does each clip necessarily have a visually contradicted event to label?

The activity calls for visually contradicted event labels across the 1,200 clips, but does not say that every clip contains such an event. It also does not state how many labels of any category an individual clip receives.
Should I treat the annotation count as evidence that the model has already been trained on these clips?

No. This node describes an annotation activity, not completed annotations or model training. The specific activity is to annotate 1,200 SilentSound-MR clips with visible-event onset frames, reference-supported sound alternatives, and visually contradicted event labels.
What does SilentSound-MR v1 contain?

SilentSound-MR v1 is an artifact comprising 1,200 clips with frame-indexed event onsets, reference-supported sound alternatives, and visually contradicted event labels. Those are the specified contents; the artifact description does not give a file format, annotation procedure, or count of labels per clip.
What does “frame-indexed event onsets” tell me?

It says the event onsets are identified by video frame index, so the timing information is tied to frames rather than described only in general terms. It does not specify a frame rate or say that every event has an unambiguous onset.
Does the frame index itself identify what the event sounds like?

No. An event onset locates a beginning in the visual timeline; it does not uniquely determine the sound. SilentSound-MR v1 also contains reference-supported sound alternatives to represent the acoustic possibilities recorded for the clips.
Should “reference-supported sound alternatives” be read as any sound a viewer might imagine?
No. The qualification is important: the alternatives are supported by references. The artifact description does not say that every imaginable or merely plausible sound is included.
Do the alternatives imply one clip has multiple equally correct soundtracks?

The description identifies sound alternatives supported by references, but it does not assign equal status to them, specify how many occur for a given clip, or define complete soundtracks. It is safer to understand them as annotated alternatives without adding those assumptions.
How are visually contradicted event labels different from those alternatives?

They mark events that conflict with what is visible. Reference-supported alternatives capture possibilities for sound; visually contradicted event labels identify a different category—events the visual evidence contradicts. Acoustic uncertainty should not be confused with visual contradiction.
If the video cannot tell two sounds apart, would that make either of them visually contradicted?

Not on that basis alone. A video's inability to uniquely determine a sound is not the same as showing that an event did not occur. The distinction between alternatives and visually contradicted events is central to what these labels express.
Could an event have a frame-indexed onset and still be visually contradicted?

Those annotations answer different questions: an onset identifies when an event begins in the frames, while a contradiction label concerns whether a proposed event conflicts with the visuals. The artifact description does not specify how individual onset records and contradiction labels are linked, so it does not establish that any particular event has both.
Is the 1,200 figure the number of annotated alternatives?
No. It is the number of clips in SilentSound-MR v1. The description does not state a total number of event onsets, sound alternatives, or visually contradicted event labels.
Does the “v1” name tell us what changed from another version?
No. “SilentSound-MR v1” is the artifact's name here. Its description does not give a version history or a comparison with any other release.
Can I infer a particular annotation schema from the word “labels”?

Only that visually contradicted events are labeled. The description does not specify label vocabulary, storage format, adjudication rules, or how the three kinds of information are organized within a clip.
What is the value of having these three kinds of information together?

They keep distinct aspects of the silent-video audio problem visible in one artifact: frame-indexed onsets concern timing, reference-supported alternatives concern acoustic possibilities, and visually contradicted event labels concern conflicts with the video. Their presence does not, by itself, establish any model's performance on those aspects.
So calling SilentSound-MR v1 an artifact doesn't mean a particular model has met the timing or alternative-coverage targets?
Correct. The artifact description specifies 1,200 clips and their three annotation categories. It does not report onset error, alternative recall, contradiction rate, or a model comparison.
What is the next activity for SilentSound-MR v1?

Audit the SilentSound-MR v1 labels, train matched-size diffusion and deterministic models, and measure held-out onset mean absolute error (MAE), alternative recall, and contradiction rate. This describes the work to do, not completed training or results.
Why audit the labels before measuring anything?

The measurements depend on the artifact's annotations. Auditing its labels is a way to examine the material those measurements will rely on. The activity does not specify an audit procedure or say what the audit will find.
Which labels are relevant here?

SilentSound-MR v1 contains frame-indexed event onsets, reference-supported sound alternatives, and visually contradicted event labels. Those correspond to the three aspects measured later: onset MAE, alternative recall, and contradiction rate.
Does an audit mean changing the labels?
Not necessarily. The activity says to audit them; it does not report errors, prescribe revisions, or state that any labels will change.
What is being matched between the two models?
